concepts.title: Checked vs Unchecked Exceptions
concepts.description: Java's exception hierarchy splits into checked exceptions, which the compiler forces every caller to either handle or declare, and unchecked exceptions, which it doesn't -- a distinction rooted not in severity, but in whether a failure is an anticipated, recoverable condition external to your code or a bug in the code itself.
learningObjectives: Describe Java's Throwable hierarchy and where Error, Exception, and RuntimeException each sit within it.
Explain the precise compile-time rule that distinguishes a checked exception from an unchecked one.
Use throws to declare a checked exception a method might propagate, and explain what happens if you don't.
Explain the design rationale for the checked/unchecked split: recoverable external conditions vs programming bugs.
Identify common checked exceptions (IOException) and unchecked exceptions (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) from the standard library.
Critique the anti-pattern of catching a checked exception only to silently swallow it.

sections.heading: The Throwable Hierarchy: Error, Exception, and RuntimeException
sections.body:
Everything that can be thrown and caught in Java is a subclass of `Throwable`. `Throwable` has two direct subclasses, and they mean genuinely different things. `Error` represents serious problems the JVM itself is signaling -- things like `OutOfMemoryError` or `StackOverflowError` -- that ordinary application code generally has no realistic way to recover from and is not expected to catch. `Exception` is the base for conditions that a program might reasonably want to catch and respond to.

Under `Exception`, there's a further, load-bearing split: `RuntimeException` and everything that extends it are **unchecked**. Every other subclass of `Exception` -- one that does *not* extend `RuntimeException` -- is **checked**. `Error` and its subclasses are also unchecked, for what it's worth, even though they sit outside `Exception` entirely.

```text
Throwable
├── Error                     (unchecked -- OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
└── Exception
    ├── IOException            (checked)
    ├── SQLException           (checked)
    └── RuntimeException       (unchecked)
        ├── NullPointerException
        ├── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
        ├── IllegalArgumentException
        └── ArithmeticException
```

It's worth internalizing this tree precisely, because the checked/unchecked label is not a property the compiler computes from how dangerous an exception sounds -- it's computed purely from *where a class sits in this tree*, specifically whether it descends from `RuntimeException` (or `Error`) or not.

sections.heading: The Compile-Time Rule: What Actually Makes an Exception 'Checked'
Why the Split Exists: Recoverable Conditions vs Programming Bugs
sections.body:
The checked/unchecked distinction exists to separate two very different kinds of 'things going wrong,' and to apply compiler pressure to only one of them. **Checked exceptions** are meant for conditions that are external to your program's own logic and that a well-written caller could reasonably anticipate and recover from: a file that doesn't exist, a network connection that times out, a database that's temporarily unreachable. None of these indicate a bug in the code that triggered them -- they're facts about the environment the code is running in, at a moment in time. The compiler forcing every caller to at least acknowledge the possibility is a deliberate nudge to think about these failure modes at API boundaries, rather than silently pretending they can't happen.

**Unchecked exceptions** -- overwhelmingly, subclasses of `RuntimeException` -- typically signal a bug in the code itself: dereferencing a `null` you shouldn't have, indexing past the end of an array, dividing by a value that should have been validated first. Forcing every method up an arbitrarily deep call stack to declare `throws NullPointerException` would be close to meaningless, since almost any method could theoretically NPE given sufficiently wrong input -- the checked-exception machinery only earns its cost when the set of things that can go wrong is genuinely small, specific, and worth naming in a method's public contract.

This is also why you'll see library and application code deliberately *throw* unchecked exceptions like `IllegalArgumentException` or `IllegalStateException` for misuse of an API (calling a method with an invalid argument, or in the wrong state) -- these are, by design, programmer errors on the caller's side that should be fixed in code, not conditions a caller is expected to gracefully recover from at run time.

sections.heading: throws Propagation, and the Cost of Handling It Wrong

examples.title: A Checked Exception Forces Acknowledgment at Compile Time
examples.explanation: `FileReader`'s constructor is declared to throw `FileNotFoundException`, a checked exception (a subclass of `IOException`, which is itself a subclass of `Exception` that does not extend `RuntimeException`). Because `openBroken` neither wraps the call in a `try`/`catch` nor declares `throws` on its own signature, `javac` refuses to produce any bytecode at all for this class -- the program never runs in this broken state, which is exactly the point of a checked exception. `openFixed` satisfies the compiler by declaring `throws IOException`, which is honest about the fact that opening a file can fail for reasons entirely outside this method's control, and pushes the decision of how to actually respond to that failure up to whoever calls `openFixed`.

examples.title: Unchecked Exceptions Compile Fine Without Any Declaration
examples.explanation: `divide` compiles without a single complaint, even though dividing by zero is a real, reachable failure mode -- `ArithmeticException` extends `RuntimeException`, so it's unchecked, and the compiler never requires it to be caught or declared. Running this program prints "about to divide", then crashes with an uncaught `ArithmeticException: / by zero` before the second `println` ever executes -- the JVM prints a stack trace to standard error and the process exits with a nonzero status. Nothing about this method's signature warned a caller that this could happen; that's a deliberate consequence of the checked/unchecked split, not an oversight -- requiring every arithmetic method in existence to declare `throws ArithmeticException` would add ceremony to essentially every numeric method in the language for a condition that's fundamentally about a bad *value*, not an external, unpredictable condition.

misconceptions.description: Checked exceptions are for 'serious' failures, and unchecked exceptions are for 'minor' ones -- the split is basically about severity.
misconceptions.clarification: Severity has nothing to do with it. The split is purely structural: a checked exception is any subclass of `Exception` that does NOT also extend `RuntimeException`; everything else -- `RuntimeException` and its subclasses, plus all of `Error` and its subclasses -- is unchecked. In fact, `Error` covers some of the most severe conditions in the entire hierarchy (`OutOfMemoryError`, `StackOverflowError`), and it's unchecked. The real axis is: is this a condition external to the code, that a caller could reasonably anticipate and recover from (checked), or does it typically indicate a bug in the code itself, or a condition too pervasive to usefully name in every signature (unchecked)?

misconceptions.description: Wrapping a checked exception in a try/catch with an empty or purely log-and-continue catch block is a safe, harmless way to satisfy the compiler when you don't want to deal with it right now.
misconceptions.clarification: An empty or log-only catch block for a checked exception silences the compiler while throwing away the entire reason the exception existed: the program continues executing as if the operation had succeeded, even though it didn't. This is especially dangerous for checked exceptions specifically, because the compiler's insistence on handling them was a deliberate signal that this failure mode is real and worth thinking about -- swallowing it defeats that signal completely and tends to produce bugs that surface much later, far from the code that actually failed, and with no trace of the original cause left behind.

exercises.prompt: This code fails to compile with: `error: unreported exception java.io.IOException; must be caught or declared to be thrown`. Find the cause and fix it by propagating the checked exception correctly.
hints: Both `new FileReader(path)` and `reader.readLine()` are declared to throw checked exceptions -- neither is caught, and readFirstLine declares no throws clause at all.
You have two legitimate options: add a try/catch inside readFirstLine, or declare `throws IOException` on readFirstLine and let the caller (main) deal with it.

If you propagate with throws instead of catching, remember that main will then also need to either catch it or declare its own throws IOException, since the exception keeps propagating up the call chain.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `FileReader`'s constructor and `BufferedReader.readLine()` are both declared to throw `IOException`, a checked exception -- `javac` requires every checked exception a method's body might produce to be either caught there or declared in that method's own `throws` clause, and the original `readFirstLine` did neither. The fix declares `throws IOException` on `readFirstLine`, which is an honest statement that reading a file can fail for reasons outside this method's control (the file might not exist, a disk error might occur, and so on). Because `main` calls `readFirstLine` and doesn't catch the exception either, `main` itself now also needs `throws IOException` on its own signature -- the checked-exception obligation keeps propagating up the call chain until something actually catches it or, as here, it's allowed to propagate all the way out of main, which would print a stack trace and exit with a nonzero status if the file genuinely can't be read.

exercises.prompt: What happens when this program runs? Be specific about what prints and what does not.
hints: unitsPerBox declares no throws clause at all -- does that mean it's guaranteed not to fail, or just that the compiler isn't tracking whether it can fail?
Trace the loop through boxCounts = {5, 0, 2} one iteration at a time. What happens on the SECOND iteration specifically?
Once an exception is thrown and nothing catches it, does the loop continue to its next iteration, or does the whole program stop right there?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'Calculating units per box...', then 'Result: 20' for boxCount=5, then throws an uncaught ArithmeticException (/ by zero) on boxCount=0 -- the program terminates immediately with a stack trace on standard error. 'Result: 50' (for boxCount=2) and 'Done.' never print.
exercises.solutionExplanation: unitsPerBox's body divides by boxCount, an operation that compiles fine because ArithmeticException is unchecked (it extends RuntimeException), so the compiler never requires it to be declared or caught -- that says nothing about whether it can actually happen at run time. The loop's first iteration, boxCount = 5, computes 100 / 5 = 20 without issue, printing 'Result: 20'. The second iteration, boxCount = 0, throws ArithmeticException: / by zero the moment the division executes; since nothing anywhere in this call chain catches it, it propagates all the way out of unitsPerBox, out of main, and out of the program entirely -- the JVM prints a stack trace to standard error and the process exits with a nonzero status. Execution never reaches the loop's third iteration (boxCount = 2) or the final 'Done.' print, because an uncaught exception stops the entire program at the point it occurred, not just the current loop iteration.

assessments.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what determines whether an exception class is 'checked' or 'unchecked' in Java?
options: Checked exceptions represent more severe failures than unchecked exceptions.
An exception is unchecked if it extends RuntimeException (or is an Error); every other subclass of Exception is checked, and the compiler enforces handling only for the checked ones.
Any exception you create yourself with a custom class is automatically unchecked, while only exceptions from the standard library can be checked.
Checked exceptions are checked by the JVM at run time, while unchecked exceptions are only checked by the compiler.
assessments.explanation: Option B states the actual rule precisely: the checked/unchecked label is determined entirely by where a class sits in the Throwable hierarchy -- specifically whether it descends from RuntimeException (or is an Error), not by severity. Option A is the classic misconception this concept directly addresses; Error, which is unchecked, covers some of the most severe failures in the JVM. Option C is wrong -- a custom exception class is checked or unchecked based purely on which class it extends (Exception vs RuntimeException), regardless of who wrote it. Option D has the terminology backwards: it's precisely the OPPOSITE of what 'checked' means here -- checked exceptions are checked by the COMPILER (at compile time, via javac), while unchecked exceptions receive no such compile-time enforcement at all, though both kinds are of course still capable of being thrown and caught at run time.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer asks why Java bothers distinguishing checked from unchecked exceptions at all, and specifically why the compiler doesn't just force every method to declare every exception it could possibly throw, including things like NullPointerException. Explain the reasoning behind the split.
assessments.modelAnswer: The checked/unchecked split exists to apply the compiler's enforcement selectively, to the kinds of failures where that enforcement is actually useful, rather than universally. Checked exceptions are meant to represent conditions that are external to the code's own logic and that a well-written caller could reasonably anticipate and recover from -- a file that doesn't exist, a network call that times out, a database that's briefly unreachable. These are facts about the environment at a particular moment, not defects in the code, and there's real value in the compiler forcing every caller along the chain to at least acknowledge that the operation might fail, rather than letting that possibility be silently ignored. Unchecked exceptions, by contrast, are overwhelmingly subclasses of RuntimeException, and they typically signal a genuine bug in the code -- dereferencing something that shouldn't have been null, indexing past an array's bounds, dividing by a value that should have been validated first. If Java required every method to declare throws NullPointerException the moment it dereferenced any object, or throws ArithmeticException the moment it divided two numbers, that requirement would apply to nearly every method in existence, since almost any method can theoretically be called with bad enough input to trigger one of these. The throws clause would balloon into a list of 'basically anything could go wrong here' on every single method signature, which would convey essentially no useful information to a reader and would make the genuinely meaningful, specific checked exceptions -- the ones actually worth designing an API around -- disappear into that noise. So the split is really a judgment call, baked into the language, about where compiler-enforced acknowledgment earns its cost (specific, external, recoverable conditions) and where it would just add ceremony without adding useful signal (pervasive conditions that are really about incorrect code, not about the environment).

assessments.prompt: A library method is declared as public void loadConfig(String path) throws IOException. A later release changes it to public void loadConfig(String path) throws IOException, SQLException. What is the consequence for existing callers?
options: None -- adding a new checked exception to a throws clause is always fully backward compatible with existing code.

Every existing caller that doesn't already catch or declare SQLException now fails to compile, because throws is part of a method's public contract, and adding a new checked exception is a breaking change for code compiled against the old signature.
Existing already-compiled .class files calling the old version will start throwing SQLException automatically at run time, without needing to recompile at all.
This change is illegal, and javac refuses to compile the library itself, since a throws clause can never be modified once a method has been published.
assessments.explanation: A throws clause is part of a method's public contract, exactly like its parameter types and return type -- callers compiled against the old signature only ever acknowledged IOException, and adding SQLException to the signature means those callers now have an unacknowledged checked exception their code doesn't handle, which javac flags as a compile error the next time they're rebuilt against the new signature. Option A ignores this real, common source of breaking API changes. Option C misunderstands how already-compiled bytecode works -- it isn't retroactively altered by a signature change elsewhere. Option D is wrong because changing a throws clause is completely legal from the compiler's point of view; the cost falls on callers, not on the library itself.

assessments.prompt: try { loadConfig("app.config"); } catch (IOException e) { } What is the most accurate critique of this code?
options: It's a fully safe way to satisfy the compiler when a method can't recover from a checked exception -- there's no real downside, since the exception type is at least named in the catch clause.

It compiles and technically satisfies javac's requirement, but it silently discards the entire reason the checked exception existed -- the program continues in a broken state (config never actually loaded) with no trace of why, which is exactly the anti-pattern checked exceptions are meant to prevent.
It fails to compile, because a catch block handling a checked exception must contain at least one executable statement.
It's functionally equivalent to declaring throws IOException on the enclosing method, since both approaches satisfy the compiler in the same way.
assessments.explanation: An empty catch block compiles and stops the compiler from complaining, but it throws away the information the checked exception was carrying -- the program proceeds as though loadConfig succeeded even though it didn't, with nothing logged and no trace left behind for anyone debugging the resulting broken state later. Option A is precisely the misconception this material warns against; naming the exception type in a catch clause that does nothing provides zero actual safety. Option C is wrong -- an empty catch block is completely legal Java, however inadvisable. Option D is wrong because declaring throws propagates the exception to a caller who might actually handle it, while swallowing it here makes it vanish entirely -- these have opposite effects on whether the failure is ever visible to anyone.

assessments.prompt: Two methods might each fail: (1) one calls Integer.parseInt(text), which can throw NumberFormatException; (2) one calls new FileInputStream(path), which can throw FileNotFoundException. Which of these, if either, would the compiler actually require to be caught or declared with throws?
options: Only (1), because NumberFormatException is checked while FileNotFoundException is unchecked.

Only (2), because FileNotFoundException extends IOException, which does not extend RuntimeException and is therefore checked; NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException, making it unchecked and requiring no such declaration.
Both (1) and (2), since any exception that can realistically occur in a method's body must be declared or caught.
Neither (1) nor (2), since the compiler only enforces this rule for exceptions raised directly with a throw statement, not ones thrown from inside library methods.
assessments.explanation: The checked/unchecked distinction depends entirely on where a class sits in the Throwable hierarchy. FileNotFoundException is a subclass of IOException, which is a subclass of Exception that does not extend RuntimeException -- so it's checked, and a method whose body might produce it must catch or declare it. NumberFormatException, by contrast, is a subclass of IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException -- so it's unchecked, and the compiler enforces nothing about it regardless of how likely it is to actually occur. Option A has the two exactly backwards. Option C is wrong because unchecked exceptions never require this regardless of likelihood. Option D is wrong -- the compiler's enforcement applies to any checked exception a method's body might produce, whether via a direct throw or by calling another method (including a library method) that's declared to throw one.

concepts.title: try, catch, and finally: Handling Exceptions and Building Custom Ones
concepts.description: try/catch matches a thrown exception to the most specific applicable handler in top-to-bottom order, finally runs no matter how the try block actually ends -- including in a genuinely surprising interaction with return -- and custom exception classes let you give your own failure conditions a name, a message, and a preserved cause.
learningObjectives: Write a try/catch block with multiple catch clauses in the correct order and explain why order matters.
Use multi-catch (catch (A | B e)) to handle multiple unrelated exception types with shared logic.
Explain precisely when a finally block executes relative to return statements and thrown exceptions.
Predict the surprising outcome of a return statement inside both a try block and its finally block.
Define a custom exception class, choosing checked vs unchecked appropriately, with proper constructors and a chained cause.

sections.heading: try and catch: Matching an Exception to the Right Handler
Multi-Catch: One Handler for Several Unrelated Types
finally: Runs No Matter What -- Including a Genuinely Surprising Case with return
Designing Custom Exception Classes

examples.title: Catch Order Matters: The Compiler Rejects an Unreachable catch
examples.explanation: In the broken version, `ArithmeticException` is a subtype of `Exception`, so the first catch clause -- `catch (Exception e)` -- already matches every `ArithmeticException` that could ever be thrown here, along with anything else that extends `Exception`. That makes the second catch clause permanently unreachable: there's no possible exception that could reach it, since anything it would match was already claimed by the broader clause above. `javac` recognizes this statically and refuses to compile it, rather than letting it silently become dead code. The fixed version simply lists the narrower, more specific type first -- `ArithmeticException` gets its own targeted handling, and `Exception` remains as a genuine fallback for anything else, which is the general rule for ordering catch clauses: most specific to least specific, top to bottom.

examples.title: finally Runs No Matter What -- Even Silently Overriding a return
examples.explanation: The try block prints its message and evaluates return 1, but that return does not complete the method immediately -- Java always runs the finally block first, before actually handing control back to the caller. The finally block prints its own message and then executes return 2, which completes compute() right then and there; the pending return 1 from the try block is discarded, having never actually taken effect. The program therefore prints both messages, followed by 'result = 2', not 'result = 1'. This is precisely why placing a return (or throw) inside a finally block is considered a serious anti-pattern in real code: it can silently override the intended result of the try block, or silently swallow an exception that was actively propagating out of it, with zero warning from the compiler.

examples.title: A Custom Checked Exception That Preserves Its Cause
examples.explanation: InsufficientFundsException extends Exception directly, making it a checked exception -- a deliberate choice here, since 'the account doesn't have enough money' is exactly the kind of anticipated, recoverable business condition checked exceptions are meant for, not a programming bug. Because withdraw declares throws InsufficientFundsException, javac forces main to either catch it or declare its own throws -- main catches it and prints a clear message built from getMessage(), the text passed to the exception's constructor. The second constructor, taking a Throwable cause, isn't exercised in this particular example, but it exists precisely so that if a future version of withdraw needed to wrap a lower-level failure (say, a database error while checking the balance) into this same, more meaningful exception type, the original cause could be preserved and inspected later via getCause() rather than being discarded.

misconceptions.description: Since only one catch block can ever run for a given exception, the order the catch clauses are written in doesn't really matter -- Java will find the right one regardless.
misconceptions.clarification: Order matters critically, precisely because only one catch block runs: Java checks catch clauses strictly top to bottom and executes the body of the FIRST one whose type matches, then stops looking entirely. If a broader supertype is listed before a narrower subtype of it, the narrower catch block becomes permanently unreachable -- every exception it could ever match was already claimed by the broader clause above it -- and this specific situation is caught by the compiler as an error, not silently accepted. The safe rule is to always order catch clauses from most specific to least specific.

misconceptions.description: finally is basically just a place for cleanup code that runs after the try/catch finishes -- equivalent to writing that same code right after the whole try/catch statement.
misconceptions.clarification: finally is not equivalent to code placed after the try/catch block, in two specific, important ways. First, finally runs even when the try or catch block executes a return statement -- the return is paused, finally runs, and only then does the method actually complete (unless finally itself returns or throws, in which case it overrides the pending outcome). Code placed after the try/catch would never run in that case at all, because the method would have already exited via the earlier return. Second, finally runs even when an exception is thrown and not caught by any of the try's catch blocks -- it still executes on the way out, before the exception continues propagating to the caller -- whereas code placed after the try/catch would never be reached in that scenario, since control never reaches past the point where the uncaught exception escaped.

exercises.prompt: This code fails to compile with: `error: exception NumberFormatException has already been caught`. Explain why, and fix the ordering.
hints: Check the class hierarchy: does NumberFormatException extend RuntimeException, or is it unrelated to it?
The first catch clause here is broader than the second -- would every NumberFormatException that could occur already be caught by the first clause?
Reorder the catch clauses so the more specific type, NumberFormatException, comes before the more general RuntimeException.
exercises.solutionExplanation: NumberFormatException extends IllegalArgumentException, which extends RuntimeException -- so it is a subtype of RuntimeException, not an unrelated type. The original code lists catch (RuntimeException e) first, which already matches every NumberFormatException that Integer.parseInt could ever throw, making the second, narrower catch clause permanently unreachable -- there's no exception left for it to catch that the first clause wouldn't have already claimed. javac detects this statically and refuses to compile. Swapping the order so NumberFormatException is listed first fixes it: now the more specific, more informative handler runs for actual number-format failures, and the broader RuntimeException clause remains as a genuine fallback for any other unchecked exception Integer.parseInt might theoretically throw.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and what value does it actually return from validate()? Explain the surprising part.
hints: input is -5, so the try block throws IllegalArgumentException before it ever reaches its own return true.
The catch block handles the exception and evaluates return false -- but does that return statement actually complete the method immediately?
finally runs after the catch block's return is evaluated but before the method truly exits -- and this finally block has its own return statement. Which one wins?
exercises.expectedAnswer: It prints 'checking input: -5', then 'caught: negative input', then 'cleanup running', then 'result: true'. Even though the catch block evaluates return false, the finally block's own return true executes afterward and overrides it -- validate() actually returns true, not false.
exercises.solutionExplanation: With input = -5, the try block prints its message and then throws IllegalArgumentException before reaching return true. The catch clause matches, prints 'caught: negative input', and evaluates return false -- but that return is only a pending outcome, not a completed one, because finally must still run before the method can actually exit. finally prints 'cleanup running' and then executes its own return true, which completes the method right there, discarding the catch block's pending return false entirely. So validate(-5) actually returns true, and main prints 'result: true' -- a direct, sharper illustration of the same finally-overrides-return trap: it's not limited to overriding a try block's return, it overrides a catch block's return via the exact same mechanism, which is precisely why a return inside finally is considered dangerous regardless of which earlier block it's overriding.

options: 10, because the try block's return statement executes and completes the method before finally ever runs.
20, because finally always runs before the method actually completes, and its own return statement overrides the try block's pending return.
This fails to compile, because a method cannot have return statements in both try and finally.
It throws an exception at runtime because two return statements conflict.
assessments.explanation: Option B correctly describes the mechanism: finally always runs after the try block, before the method's completion is finalized -- even when that completion would have been a return statement. Since the finally block here itself contains a return statement, that return executes and completes the method, discarding the try block's pending return 10 entirely, so f() returns 20. Option A is the natural but incorrect assumption that a return statement in try immediately and unconditionally exits the method -- it doesn't, when a finally block is present. Option C is wrong because this code compiles perfectly fine; having return statements in both try and finally is legal Java, just widely considered poor practice. Option D is wrong because there is no runtime conflict or exception here at all -- the behavior is fully deterministic and specified by the language, just frequently surprising to newcomers.

assessments.prompt: Explain the finally-overrides-return trap to a colleague who just discovered it in their own code, and separately explain why a well-designed custom exception class should provide a constructor that accepts a Throwable cause.
assessments.modelAnswer: The finally-overrides-return trap happens because finally is guaranteed to run before a method's execution actually finishes, no matter how the try or catch block was about to finish -- including via a return statement. When try (or catch) executes return, that return is more like a pending outcome than a completed action: Java still has to run the finally block before that outcome is finalized. If the finally block itself contains a return (or a throw), that statement completes the method right there, and whatever the try or catch block was about to return is simply discarded, with absolutely no warning from the compiler. This is dangerous specifically because it looks completely reasonable at a glance -- both blocks return a value, and it is not obvious from casually reading the code which one 'wins' unless you already know this specific rule. The fix is behavioral, not syntactic: treat finally as a place exclusively for side-effect cleanup -- closing resources, releasing locks, logging -- and never put a return or throw inside one. On the custom exception question: a constructor that accepts a Throwable cause, typically alongside a String message, lets you wrap a lower-level exception in a more meaningful, higher-level one without losing the original failure's identity and stack trace. If a method catches a low-level exception like SQLException and wants to re-throw something more meaningful to its own callers, like OrderProcessingException, throwing it WITHOUT passing the original exception as a cause means that anyone who later prints the stack trace or calls getCause() on the new exception sees nothing about the SQLException that actually triggered the problem -- exactly the debugging information you'd want most when something fails in production. Providing that (message, cause) constructor, and consistently using it whenever you're wrapping an underlying failure, costs almost nothing and preserves a genuinely important diagnostic trail.

assessments.prompt: Which of these two multi-catch declarations fails to compile, and why? (A) catch (SQLException | IOException e) { ... } (B) catch (FileNotFoundException | IOException e) { ... }
options: (A) fails to compile, because SQLException and IOException share no common supertype other than Exception itself.

(B) fails to compile, because FileNotFoundException is itself a subtype of IOException -- the second alternative in the pair can never add anything the first doesn't already cover, and Java specifically disallows multi-catching a type alongside one of its own subtypes.
Both (A) and (B) fail to compile, since multi-catch can only ever combine two unrelated subtypes of RuntimeException specifically.
Neither fails to compile; both are completely valid multi-catch declarations as written.
assessments.explanation: Multi-catch requires that neither listed type be a subtype of the other, since that would make one alternative entirely redundant -- (B) violates this directly, because FileNotFoundException extends IOException, so every exception the first alternative could match is already covered by the second. (A) is perfectly legal multi-catch: SQLException and IOException have no subtype relationship to each other, which is exactly the situation multi-catch exists for. Option A is wrong about which pair is actually the problem. Option C invents a restriction to RuntimeException subtypes that doesn't exist -- multi-catch works with checked exception types too, as (A) demonstrates. Option D is wrong because (B) is a genuine compile error.

assessments.prompt: try { Object[] items = new String[3]; items[0] = 42; } catch (ArrayStoreException e) { System.out.println("store error"); } catch (RuntimeException e) { System.out.println("runtime error"); } catch (Exception e) { System.out.println("general error"); } Given that ArrayStoreException extends RuntimeException, what happens when this is compiled and run?
options: It compiles fine and prints "store error", because ArrayStoreException is listed first and is the most specific type matching the exception actually thrown by storing an int into a String array.
It fails to compile, because listing ArrayStoreException before RuntimeException before Exception, in that order, makes the later clauses unreachable.
It compiles fine but prints "runtime error" instead, because RuntimeException is always checked before any of its subtypes at run time, regardless of catch order.
It throws an uncaught exception at run time, since none of the three catch clauses can actually match a store error.
assessments.explanation: items is declared as Object[] but actually refers to a String[] at run time; assigning items[0] = 42 (autoboxed to Integer) attempts to store an Integer into an array whose real element type is String, which throws ArrayStoreException. The catch clauses here are ordered correctly -- most specific (ArrayStoreException) first, then its broader supertype RuntimeException, then the broadest, Exception -- so this compiles fine, and since ArrayStoreException is thrown, the first, most specific matching clause runs, printing "store error". Option B misapplies the unreachable-catch rule, which only flags a narrower clause placed AFTER a broader one already covering it -- the order here is the reverse, and correct. Option C invents a run-time matching mechanism Java doesn't have; catch matching always respects the written top-to-bottom order. Option D is wrong because the first clause matches exactly.

assessments.prompt: A class is designed to signal that a withdrawal amount exceeds an account's balance -- a normal, anticipated business condition callers should be able to handle. Which custom exception design is most appropriate?
options: class InsufficientFundsException extends RuntimeException { ... } -- since callers should never be forced by the compiler to acknowledge an ordinary business condition.

class InsufficientFundsException extends Exception { ... }, with constructors accepting a message and, separately, a message plus a Throwable cause -- since this is an anticipated, recoverable external condition, making a checked exception appropriate, with both constructors delegating to super(...) for proper messages and cause-chaining.
class InsufficientFundsException extends Error { ... } -- since running out of funds is a serious problem for the account holder.
class InsufficientFundsException extends Throwable { ... } directly, bypassing both Exception and Error entirely for maximum design flexibility.
assessments.explanation: Insufficient funds is exactly the kind of anticipated, recoverable, external-to-the-code condition checked exceptions are meant for -- it's not a bug, and a caller (a UI showing an error, a batch job logging and skipping the transaction) can reasonably be expected to handle it. Extending Exception directly makes it checked, and providing both a message-only and a message-plus-cause constructor is the standard, low-cost convention that supports clear error messages now and cause-chaining if a future implementation needs to wrap a lower-level failure. Option A would let callers silently ignore a condition the design intends them to consider. Option C is wrong -- Error is reserved for serious JVM-level problems the application isn't expected to recover from, not ordinary business rule violations. Option D needlessly discards the well-understood Exception/Error distinction the rest of the language and ecosystem rely on.

concepts.title: try-with-resources and AutoCloseable
concepts.description: try-with-resources automatically closes any resource that implements AutoCloseable at the end of a block, in reverse order of declaration, even when an exception is thrown -- eliminating the two classic failure modes of manual finally-based cleanup: a null-check-guarded close() that's easy to get wrong, and a close() failure that silently destroys information about the real exception that was already propagating.
learningObjectives: Explain the resource-leak and lost-exception problems try-with-resources was introduced to solve, compared to manual close() in a finally block.
Write a try-with-resources statement with one or more resources and explain the exact order they are closed in.
Implement a custom class that implements AutoCloseable so it can be used directly in a try-with-resources statement.
Explain what a suppressed exception is, when one occurs, and how to retrieve it.
Explain why a resource used in try-with-resources must be effectively final.

examples.title: Before and After: Manual finally Cleanup vs try-with-resources
examples.explanation: The 'before' version needs reader declared and initialized to null outside the try specifically so finally can still reference it even if the FileReader constructor itself throws before reader is ever assigned a real value -- and the null check exists purely to avoid a NullPointerException in that specific failure path. If readLine() throws and close() also throws while cleaning up, the close() exception silently overwrites the readLine() exception, hiding the actual root cause. The 'after' version eliminates both concerns: the resource is declared directly in the try's parentheses, closed automatically no matter how the block exits, and if both the body and the automatic close both throw, the body's exception is preserved as primary with close()'s exception attached as suppressed rather than lost.

examples.title: Multiple Resources Close in Reverse Order
examples.explanation: The three resources are opened in the order they're declared -- A, then B, then C -- which prints 'open A', 'open B', 'open C' before the try block's body even runs. Once the body finishes ('using A, B, C'), Java closes the resources automatically in the EXACT REVERSE of that declaration order: C first, then B, then A -- printing 'close C', 'close B', 'close A'. This mirrors how these resources would typically depend on each other in real code (a later-declared resource, like a database Statement, is often built from and depends on an earlier one, like a Connection, so tearing down the more-dependent one first, before the resource it depends on, is the safer order).

examples.title: Suppressed Exceptions When close() Also Fails
examples.explanation: doWork() throws first, while the try block's body is still executing -- that RuntimeException becomes the primary exception that will eventually be caught. Before it can propagate out of the try statement, though, Java still has to run close() on the resource, and close() ALSO throws, this time an IllegalStateException. Rather than letting the close() exception silently replace the one already in flight (the old finally-block problem), try-with-resources attaches it to the primary exception as a suppressed exception. The catch block prints 'caught: work failed' -- confirming the ORIGINAL failure is still the one actually caught -- and then iterates getSuppressed() to also print 'suppressed: close failed too', so no information about either failure is lost, and it's clear which one was the real, original cause.

misconceptions.description: If an exception occurs while automatically closing a resource in try-with-resources, it silently overwrites or replaces whatever exception the try block's body itself had already thrown.
misconceptions.clarification: The opposite is true, and this is precisely the problem try-with-resources was designed to fix. If the try body throws an exception AND the automatic close() call also throws, the body's exception is preserved as the PRIMARY exception that actually propagates -- the exception from close() is attached to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed(), rather than being lost or silently overwriting anything. (If only close() throws, with the body completing normally, then that close() exception is simply the one that propagates, since there's no earlier exception for it to be suppressed under.)

misconceptions.description: Any object can be used in a try-with-resources statement as long as it happens to have a method literally named close().
misconceptions.clarification: The compiler requires the resource's declared type to actually implement java.lang.AutoCloseable (or its subinterface Closeable) -- having a method that happens to be spelled close(), without formally implementing that interface, is not enough and produces a compile-time error like 'incompatible types: ClassName cannot be converted to AutoCloseable'. This is a structural, interface-based requirement, not a naming convention the compiler pattern-matches against.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to safely read and print a file's first line, closing the reader no matter what happens. Instead, it can throw a NullPointerException from inside the finally block itself when the file doesn't exist. Find the bug and fix it using try-with-resources.
hints: If `new FileReader(path)` throws (because the file doesn't exist), does `reader` ever get assigned a real value before control jumps to finally?
finally still runs even when the try block's own initialization line throws -- what does reader.close() do if reader is still null at that point?
Rewrite this using try-with-resources, declaring the BufferedReader directly in the try's parentheses, and remove the manual finally block entirely.
exercises.solutionExplanation: In the original code, if `new FileReader(path)` throws (for example, FileNotFoundException because the path doesn't exist), that exception happens while reader still holds its initial value of null -- the assignment to reader never completes. Control then jumps to finally, which unconditionally calls reader.close(), and since reader is still null at that point, this throws NullPointerException, masking the original, more meaningful FileNotFoundException entirely. The try-with-resources version sidesteps this class of bug completely: the resource is declared and initialized directly in the try's own parentheses, and Java only attempts to close a resource that was actually successfully initialized in the first place -- if the FileReader construction itself fails, there's no resource to close at all, and the original exception propagates cleanly with nothing extra masking it.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and in what order? Pay close attention to the order resources are opened versus closed.
hints: Resources are opened strictly in the order they're declared inside the parentheses -- outer first, then inner.
The try block's body runs fully before either resource is closed at all.
Resources are closed in the EXACT REVERSE of the order they were opened -- which one gets closed first?
exercises.expectedAnswer:
[open] outer
[open] inner
[outer] starting work
[inner] doing detail work
[close] inner
[close] outer
done
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two resources are constructed in declaration order, so 'outer' opens before 'inner': '[open] outer' then '[open] inner'. The try block's body then runs completely, printing both log lines: '[outer] starting work' and '[inner] doing detail work'. Once the body finishes, Java automatically closes the resources in the exact REVERSE of their declaration order -- inner (opened second) is closed first, then outer (opened first) is closed last: '[close] inner' then '[close] outer'. Finally, 'done' prints after the entire try-with-resources statement, including all of its automatic closing, has completed.

assessments.prompt: Inside a try-with-resources block, the body throws a RuntimeException, and the automatic close() call on the resource also throws an exception while cleaning up. What actually happens?
options: The exception from close() replaces the original RuntimeException entirely, and only the close() exception is ever visible to the caller.
The original RuntimeException from the body propagates as the primary exception, with the exception from close() attached to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed().
Both exceptions are silently discarded, and the try-with-resources statement simply completes as if nothing had gone wrong.
The program deadlocks, because two exceptions cannot be resolved during the same try-with-resources statement.
assessments.explanation: Option B describes the actual, specified behavior: try-with-resources treats the body's exception as primary and propagates it, attaching any exception from the automatic close() call as a suppressed exception rather than losing it -- this is precisely the improvement over manual finally-based cleanup, where a failing close() inside finally really could silently replace an exception already propagating from the try block. Option A describes exactly that older, manual-cleanup failure mode, which try-with-resources specifically fixes. Option C is wrong -- neither exception is discarded; the primary one propagates and the second is preserved as suppressed information on it. Option D is fabricated -- there's no deadlock mechanism involved in exception handling here at all.

assessments.prompt: Explain to someone still manually closing resources in finally blocks why try-with-resources is considered strictly safer, referencing both the closing order for multiple resources and the concept of a suppressed exception.
assessments.modelAnswer: Manual cleanup in a finally block has two recurring problems: you need a null check before calling close(), because the resource's own construction might have failed before it was ever assigned, and if close() itself throws while an exception from the try block is already propagating, that close() exception silently overwrites the original one -- so whoever eventually handles the exception sees only the (often less informative) cleanup failure, with no trace of the real root cause that actually triggered the whole situation. try-with-resources addresses both issues directly. First, the resource is declared and initialized inside the try statement's own parentheses, and Java only ever attempts to close a resource that was actually successfully constructed -- if construction itself fails, there's no partially-initialized resource lying around for a finally block to mishandle with a null check. Second, when the try body throws AND the automatic close() also throws, Java doesn't let the close() exception silently replace the original -- it keeps the body's exception as the primary one that actually propagates to the caller, and attaches the close() exception to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable through getSuppressed(). Nothing is lost; a careful caller can inspect both the primary failure and whatever went wrong during cleanup. On the ordering question: when a try-with-resources statement declares multiple resources, they're closed in the exact reverse of the order they were opened in -- the most-recently-opened, and typically most-dependent, resource is torn down first, mirroring how such resources usually relate to each other (a Statement built from a Connection should be closed before that Connection is, for instance). All of this happens automatically and correctly every time, without the programmer having to hand-write and re-verify the null checks, ordering, and exception-preservation logic that manual finally-based cleanup requires getting right by hand, every single time.

assessments.prompt: class Widget { public void close() { System.out.println("closing"); } } -- Widget does NOT implement AutoCloseable. try (Widget w = new Widget()) { } What happens when this is compiled?
options: It compiles fine, because Widget has a method literally named close(), and that alone is all try-with-resources actually requires.

It fails to compile, because the compiler requires the resource's declared type to actually implement java.lang.AutoCloseable (or Closeable) -- merely having a same-named close() method, without formally implementing that interface, does not satisfy the requirement.
It compiles fine but never actually calls close() at run time, since Widget isn't a recognized built-in resource type.
It fails to compile, but only because Widget's close() method fails to declare throws Exception.
assessments.explanation: try-with-resources is a structural, interface-based mechanism -- the compiler checks that the declared type of the resource actually implements AutoCloseable (or its subinterface Closeable), not merely that it happens to have a method spelled close(). Widget has the right method name but no formal implements clause, so the compiler rejects this with an incompatible-types error. Option A describes a naming-convention check the compiler does not perform. Option C is wrong because this code doesn't compile at all, so nothing about it ever reaches run time. Option D is wrong -- AutoCloseable's close() is declared to throw Exception, but an implementing class is always free to narrow that to no declared exception at all, which is exactly what Widget's close() does; that's not the actual problem here.

assessments.prompt: class CleanResource implements AutoCloseable { void doWork() { System.out.println("working"); } public void close() { throw new IllegalStateException("close failed"); } } try (CleanResource r = new CleanResource()) { r.doWork(); } What happens?
options: The try statement completes with no visible effect at all, since the body itself never threw anything.

IllegalStateException("close failed") propagates out of the try statement as an ordinary, unsuppressed exception -- since the body completed normally, there's no earlier exception for close()'s failure to be attached to as suppressed; it simply is the exception that propagates.
The exception from close() is automatically suppressed and discarded, since suppression applies to any exception thrown by an automatic close() call.
This throws a NullPointerException, because a resource cannot be closed unless something in the try body already failed first.
assessments.explanation: doWork() runs and completes normally, printing "working" -- no exception is in flight from the body at all. When close() is then called automatically and throws IllegalStateException, there is no primary exception already propagating for it to be suppressed under, so it simply becomes the exception that propagates out of the try statement, exactly as if it had been thrown directly. Option A ignores that close()'s own exception still has to go somewhere. Option C misapplies suppression -- suppression only happens specifically when BOTH the body and close() throw; a lone close() failure is never suppressed, since suppression is additive information attached to a primary exception that doesn't exist here. Option D invents a precondition on closing that Java's try-with-resources doesn't have -- close() always runs at the end of the block, body failure or not.
